sources.cite: Caterisano A, Decker D, Snyder B, et al. CSCCa and NSCA Joint Consensus Guidelines for Transition Periods: Safe Return to Training Following Inactivity. Strength Cond J. 2019;41(3)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch with quotes (first 100,000 of 127,339 characters): after 2 weeks or more of inactivity, conditioning 'phased in gradually and progressively'; the 50/30/20/10 rule (returning athletes at least 50% less volume in week 1 and 30% less in week 2; new athletes 50, 30, 20, 10% over four weeks); weight training work-to-rest 1:4 or more in week 1, 1:3 in week 2, at least 1:2 after; no more than 3 days of weight training in the first week; heat acclimatization over 7-14 days, exertional heat stroke cooled to 38.9 C (102 F) or less within 30 minutes of collapse, cold-water immersion fastest; sickle cell trait raises the risk of collapse and sudden death; exertional rhabdomyolysis mostly follows 'a novel workout regimen', especially after detraining, and 'Athletes who develop the symptoms associated with ER need to be quickly admitted to the hospital'.

sources.cite: NHTSA. National EMS Scope of Practice Model 2019: Including Change Notices 1.0 and 2.0 (DOT HS 813 151, 2021-08-01)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17: the record page (title, report number, date; the change notices add intramuscular injection, vaccination in a public health emergency and nasal swab collection at EMT and above) and the PDF's skill tables through a summarizing fetch whose table columns were partly unclear, so placement was checked against the course's own reading (backend/supabase/seed/labs/ems-sources.ts, 2026-11-09) and REQ-241's reading (2026-11-11). EMR: oxygen, BVM, naloxone (intranasal or auto-injector), unit-dose hazmat antidote auto-injectors, tourniquet, wound packing, emergency moves, manual stabilization; no pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring or transport. EMT adds pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring, oral glucose, aspirin, the patient's own nitroglycerin, an inhaled bronchodilator, CPAP, the epinephrine auto-injector. AEMT adds IV and IO access, non-medicated IV fluids, supraglottic airways, waveform capnography, sublingual nitroglycerin and a limited list of IV and IM drugs (dextrose, naloxone). Paramedic adds 12-lead interpretation, manual defibrillation, synchronized cardioversion, transcutaneous pacing, needle chest decompression, intubation and medicated infusions. No newer model was found on 2026-11-17.
The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles.

Her core temperature at collapse (41.3 C), its rise uncooled in the sun, and how fast each method cools her (immersion about 0.2 C a minute, ice packs 0.05, a wet sheet that traps heat 0.01) are authored FLAG figures in the order the sources give; the EMR has no thermometer and judges by mental status, as NASEMSO allows. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

brief.situation: 10:40, a charity 10K, 29 C and humid. You are an emergency medical responder at the finish-line medical tent. Runners carry in a woman, about 25, who collapsed 200 meters from the line.
handover: The tent has an ice-water tub, ice packs, sheets, water and sports drinks, and three volunteers. You have no thermometer.
An ambulance can be requested by radio; the nearest is about 10 minutes away.
Within EMR scope: assessment by hand, cooling, positioning, oxygen if available, and handover.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated seconds per real second. Pause any time.
Every assessment and treatment takes the time it would on a real call. Scene time and the drive run on the clock.
Partway through you are asked to explain your decisions in writing. The case ends when care is handed over, then a debrief scores what you did.

safetyNote: Teaching case for exam practice; fictional patient. Not medical advice; follow your local protocols and medical direction.

look.label: Primary assessment: responsiveness, airway, breathing, skin

then.log: Responds to voice with nonsense, swinging her arms; airway clear, breathing fast; skin hot, flushed and still sweating.
Alert and oriented now; skin cooler.

callAmb.label: Radio for an ambulance: suspected heat stroke, cooling under way

tub.label: Into the ice-water tub up to the chest, a volunteer holding her head and arms

effects.log: Three of you lift her into the tub; one volunteer keeps her head above the water.

packs.label: Ice packs to her neck, armpits and groin

sheet.label: Wrap her in a wet sheet and let her rest in the shade

effects.log: Wet sheet around her; it is warm within minutes.

drink.label: Give her a sports drink to sip

then.log: She gulps, chokes and coughs drink back up; her breathing turns wet and fast.

else.log: Now alert, she sips it without trouble.

airway.label: Keep her airway clear and watch her breathing as she cools

effects.log: You stay at her head, watching her breathing.

vitals.label: Pulse, blood pressure and breathing by hand

out.label: She is alert and answering clearly: out of the tub, dry her and keep watching

then.log: You take her out while she is still drowsy.

else.log: Out of the tub, alert and asking about her race.

report.label: Hand over to the ambulance crew: collapse time, confusion, cooling method and times, mental status now, vital signs

why.question: What told you this was heat stroke rather than exhaustion, and why cool here instead of waiting for the ambulance?

parts.label: Recognition
parts.criteria: Altered mental status (confusion, combativeness) in a hot runner is heat stroke, even with sweating; without a thermometer, mental status is the guide.
parts.modelAnswer: She was confused and combative with hot skin after running in the heat. Without a thermometer, the confusion is what separates heat stroke from exhaustion; sweating doesn't rule it out.

parts.label: Cool first
parts.criteria: Rapid cooling comes before transport; ice-water immersion is fastest; continue until mental status improves (no thermometer); nothing by mouth while confused; then hand over.
parts.modelAnswer: Cooling comes before transport, and the tub is the fastest. I kept her in until she was alert and talking clearly, gave nothing by mouth while she was confused, then handed over.

noProgress.rationale: She left the tent still drowsy and hot; heat stroke needs cooling before transport.

reasoningCriteria.label: Written reasoning: recognizing heat stroke and cooling first

expertPath.text: Confused, combative, hot after running in the heat: heat stroke. Into the ice tub at once; radio for an ambulance.
Primary assessment, airway watched, vital signs; nothing by mouth.
Alert and answering clearly: out, dried, handed over with times and findings.

cooled.headline: Cooled first, then handed over
cooled.body: Confusion in a hot runner is heat stroke; the tub is the fastest way to cool, and without a thermometer you cool until she is alert. That is the expert path.

late.headline: Cooled, by a slower route
late.body: She is all right, but look at how soon cooling began, the method, and when the ambulance was called.

hot.headline: Cool first, transport second
hot.body: She left still drowsy and hot. The crew can't cool her as fast as the tub could.

aspirated.headline: Nothing by mouth while confused
aspirated.body: A confused patient can't protect her airway. Fluids wait until she is alert.

scoring.modelReasoning: Confusion and combativeness with hot skin after running in the heat is heat stroke, even though she is sweating. Cool first: ice-water immersion is the fastest method, so into the tub at once while a volunteer protects her head and the ambulance is called. Without a thermometer, cool until her mental status returns to normal; give nothing by mouth while she is confused; reassess and take vital signs; then hand over with the collapse time, the cooling and the findings.

how.ask: While you cool her: with no thermometer, how do you know when to stop cooling?

choices.label: When her mental status returns to normal
After ten minutes, whatever her state

how.explain: NASEMSO: cool until below 39 C, or until mental status improves when temperature cannot be measured. Immersion is the fastest method.
